title: Write the table of bad requests

blocks.text: The outage team's validator, `check_request`, is finished: it returns the name of every rule an outage request breaks. Their test suite runs one parametrized test per row of a table, `CASES`, and the table is empty. Fill it.

`cases.py` holds the validator, its six rule names in `RULES`, and `BASE`, a valid request (every value is text, as it arrives from the form). Write `CASES`: a list of six `(row, rule)` pairs, one for each rule in `RULES`, where `row` is a request that breaks that rule. The rules:

rows: `hours` does not read as a number

blocks.text: A case is only useful if a broken check makes its test fail, so each row must break its own rule and no other. Keep weeks whole numbers, since the validator reads them with `int`. Don't change the validator or `BASE`.

"""Run executes this file. Change the calls and see what prints. Submit grades."""
import logging

# Turn the logger up, so the `log.debug` lines of your code show under the printed lines.
logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG, format="%(levelname)s %(message)s")

from cases import CASES, check_request

print("cases in the table:", len(CASES))
for row, rule in CASES:
    print(f"case named {rule}: broken rules", check_request(row))

each case is rejected for the rule it names
each case breaks its own rule and no other
the six cases name six different rules
building the cases leaves the base request unchanged
